CHAPTER 9 A New Point of View Cropping Embedded SVG Files This chapter discusses ways to control the coordinate system when you embed the SVG in a web page, changing the graphic’s scale or crop, without editing the SVG file. These SVG view options allow you to override the SVG file’s viewBox or preserveAspectRatio by modifying the URL you use to access the SVG file. There are two ways to apply views: • by using a target fragment (the part of the URL after the # or hash character) to reference the id of a element in the SVG file, or • by using the SVG view fragment syntax to directly set the view information in the URL. The chapter also covers a related technique, known as SVG stacks, which also uses URL fragments to activate different versions of the same SVG file. These techniques only apply to embedded SVG: a separate .svg file that is included as an image or object in the HTML, or an image in the CSS. They cannot be used with inline SVG markup that is part of the main HTML document, since inline SVG does not have its own URL. To change the view of an inline SVG, you need to directly edit the viewBox and preserveAspectRatio attributes, either in the markup or with JavaScript. 299 Use of these features is currently limited by a number of bugs and restrictions in WebKit/ Safari. Even in other browsers, support for views arrived later than other SVG features; older browsers may not adjust the SVG to the view, particularly when embedding images via CSS. Chapter 9
Agile Release Planning
In preparing for battle I have always found that plans are useless, but planning
is indispensable.
—Dwight D. Eisenhower
Agile planning is a commonly misunderstood part of Agile project management.
Many consider “ Agile planning” to be an oxymoron—that Agile teams plan very lit-
tle and iterate with no end in sight.
Agile planning does not call for a complete plan up front but spreads the work of
planning throughout the entire project. In fact, Agile teams spend more time plan-
ning than traditional teams; it’s just not concentrated at the start of a project.
The Solutions in This Chapter
This chapter explores the practices used to avoid the typical planning pitfalls based
on the following principles:
• Apply a higher tier of planning than Sprints: Release planning allows for a
longer planning horizon.
• Create a shared vision of the game: This ensures that everyone working on
the game understands what is being made and why.
• Enable continuing refinement of the work estimated for each feature as the
team learns more: Uncertain features can’t have precise estimates. Accuracy
can grow as the feature requirements are refined.

CHAPTER 9 Colors, Backgrounds, and Gradients Remember the first time you changed the colors of a web page? Instead of the default black text on a white background with blue links, all of a sudden you could use any combination of colors you desired—perhaps light blue text on a black background with lime green hyperlinks. From there, it was just a short hop to colored text and, eventually, even to multiple colors for the text in a page. Once you could add back‐ ground images, too, just about anything became possible, or so it seemed. Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) takes color and backgrounds even further, letting you apply many different colors and backgrounds to a single page or element, and even apply multiple backgrounds to the same element. Colors When you’re designing a page, you need to plan it out before you start. That’s gener‐ ally true in any case, but with colors, it’s even more so. If you’re going to make all hyperlinks yellow, will that clash with the background color in any part of your docu‐ ment? If you use too many colors, will the user be too overwhelmed? (Hint: yes.) If you change the default hyperlink colors, will users still be able to figure out where your links are? (For example, if you make both regular text and hyperlink text the same color, it will be much harder to spot links—in fact, almost impossible if the links aren’t underlined.) In CSS, you can set both the foreground and background colors of any element. Giving Models Texture
I
f you want a more controlled way of adjusting the look of your object than
what’s described in Chapter 8, then using material shaders alone won’t get you
there. You can use Vertex Paint, but if you’re working on a model that you
intend to animate, Vertex Paint can cause you to have many extraneous vertices
just for color. Those vertices end up slowing down the processes of rigging,
animating, and even rendering. Also, you may want to have material changes that
are independent of the topology and edge flow of your mesh.
For those sorts of scenarios, you’re going to want to use textures, which is the
focus of this chapter.
Adding Textures
Generally speaking, a texture is a kind of image that you stretch or tile over the
surface of your object to give it more detail without adding more geometry. Not
only can textures influence the color of your object, but they can also allow you to
make additional adjustments, such as stipulating the shininess of some specific
parts of the model. For example, on a human face, skin tends to be shinier across
the nose and forehead, and somewhat duller around the eyes. With textures, you
can control these sorts of things. If you’ve read through Chapter 8, then you’ve
seen some examples of that using the Gradient Texture.

The goal of automatic classification is to predict at best the class y of an object x
from some observations. A typical example is the spam filter of our mailbox, which
predicts (more or less fairly) whether a mail is a spam or not. It is omnipresent in our
daily life, by filtering the spams in our mailbox, reading automatically post-code on
our postal letters, or recognizing faces on photos that we post on social networks. It
is also very important in sciences, e.g., in medicine for early diagnosis of diseases
from high-throughput data and in the industry, e.g., for detecting potential customers
from their profiles.
In this chapter, we consider the setting of supervised classification: We have a data set
recording the label (or class) y of n observed points (or objects) x ∈ X , and we want
to build from these data a function h (x) that predicts the label of any point x ∈ X .
The function h is called a classifier. When we want to predict a label y with a function
h (x), we fall into the regression setting. Yet, the discrete nature of the labels allows
us to strongly weaken the statistical modeling of the pair (x, y) by merely requiring
that the observations (X i, Y i) i = 1,..., n are i.i.d.

we present Vapnik’s theory, which can be viewed as an analog of the model selection
problem of Chapter 2 in the context of supervised classification. Due to the discrete
nature of the labels y, the theory relies heavily on some combinatorial arguments.

The process of predictive modeling requires extensive feature engineering. It
often involves the transformation of given feature space, typically using math-
ematical functions, with the objective of reducing the modeling error for a

feature engineering. It involves domain knowledge, intuition, and most of all, a

when the data presented is not well described and labeled, effective manual
feature engineering becomes an even more prohibitive task. In this chapter,

With the requirements in place, we can step back from the lab and define what production

Understanding why production is different from a lab
A lab is idx_f6b3a080 designed to be friendly. The inputs are known, the devices are mocked, the credentials
are not real, and failure is cheap. Production is different. In production, the wrong command,
the wrong target, or the wrong summary can waste time during an incident or create a real
outage.
That does not mean network agents should never be used in real environments. It means the
first production milestone should be a controlled, read-only prototype with strong visibility.
The goal is to learn how the agent behaves under real operational conditions without giving it
permission to change the network.
A production-minded design must answer questions that a lab demo can ignore. Who called
the tool? Which device was targeted? Was the command allowed? What evidence did the agent
use? Did the system fail closed? Can another engineer replay the decision later?

Keeping the first operational step read-only
The safest first idx_6c210a34 step outside the lab is read-only operation. A read-only agent can still provide
meaningful value. It can enrich alerts, summarize BGP state, inspect interface status, check
route visibility, and prepare a clean handoff for an engineer.
Read-only does not mean risk-free. A read-only tool can still leak information, overload a
device, or produce a misleading summary. But the blast radius is much smaller than a tool that
can change configuration. That makes read-only workflows the right first milestone.
Common read-only tools include the following:
device_status for inventory and health data
interface_status for interface state and descriptions
bgp_summary for peer state and prefix counts
topology for device relationships
show_command for approved show commands
ping or reachability checks with bounded counts
Log lookup tools that return filtered events rather than raw unlimited logs
Read-only tools idx_8ddae3f6 give the team a way to evaluate usefulness before deciding whether any
recommendation or action should become more automated. That evaluation period is where
many production problems can be found safely.
Deciding what should not be automated
A useful production plan also says what the agent should not do. This is not negative thinking.
It is scope control. If the team cannot explain why a capability is safe, observable, and
recoverable, it should not be automated yet.
The most dangerous tools idx_918a2ea9 are usually the broad ones. A tool named run_command() sounds
flexible, but flexibility is exactly what makes it risky. A safer design exposes narrow tools that
describe their purpose and validate their inputs before doing anything.

Handling secrets and credentials
Secrets are where many automation projects become risky. A production agent should never
receive idx_0dca8064 credentials through a prompt. Credentials should not be hard-coded in Python files,
committed to GitHub, printed in logs, or echoed back in model output.
The preferred pattern is to keep credentials outside the code. Use environment variables, a
secrets manager, or a platform-specific credential store. Use service accounts with the least-
privilege access needed for the tool. Start with read-only credentials before any account is
allowed to change state.
For this book, the labs stay mocked, which is exactly why they are safe to run. In production,
secrets handling becomes part of the architecture, not an afterthought. The tool should receive
a credential reference or session from a trusted runtime, not ask the model what password to
use.

AWS CodeArtifact: Your centralized package repository
Modern applications are built on a software supply chain that relies heavily on open source
packages idx_7c79a644 and internal libraries. Managing these dependencies can be a headache, introducing
risks related to security and availability. AWS CodeArtifact solves this by providing a private,
managed repository that integrates with common package managers such as npm, Maven, pip,
and NuGet. Instead of your build process pulling packages directly from public repositories, it
fetches them from your private CodeArtifact warehouse. You can configure your CodeArtifact
repository to pull from public sources (such as npmjs or Maven Central) as upstreams. When a
package is requested for the first time, CodeArtifact fetches it and stores a secure copy. All
subsequent requests are served from this internal cache. This provides critical advantages in
security and compliance by giving you a single, approved source for all packages. It also
improves reliability, as your builds are no longer dependent on the availability of public
repositories. Furthermore, it enables centralization, allowing your teams to publish and share
internal libraries in one place, simplifying collaboration.
You've built your application with CodeBuild and stored your artifacts securely with
CodeArtifact. Now comes the moment of truth: getting that code safely into production
without causing downtime or breaking your application. This is where deployment
automation becomes essential.

The pressure to move quickly is real. Once a demo looks useful, people naturally ask whether it
can do more. That is exactly when shortcuts become tempting.

create problems later.
Use these questions when a shortcut is proposed:
Does this increase the blast radius?
Would this make an incident harder to investigate?
Does this bypass an existing change or access control process?
Can this be replaced by a narrower read-only tool?
Can this wait until after the pilot has produced evidence?
Would we be comfortable documenting this shortcut in the runbook?

the first pilot is to learn safely, not to prove that the agent can do everything at once.

Critical words that change the answer
Words such as not, least, best, first, most likely, and completely change the task. A candidate
may know the technology idx_ccba322d and still select the wrong option by reading past one qualifier. Slow
down when a question uses a negative or asks for an order of operations.
Best and first deserve special attention. The best long-term fix may not be the first diagnostic
step. Replacing a node might eventually resolve a hardware fault, but the first step is usually to
gather evidence. Likewise, several options may improve performance, but only one may
directly address the stated bottleneck.
Absolute terms such as always and never are often too broad for infrastructure scenarios.
Technology choices depend on workload, scale, cost, topology, and operating model. An option
that ignores those conditions should be treated carefully even when it contains a familiar
product name.
After identifying the qualifier, the next task is to locate the contextual signal that points to the
relevant technology layer.
Context signals and technology boundaries
Context tells you which part of the stack matters. Kubernetes suggests scheduling, resource
requests, the device plugin, GPU Operator, Helm, namespaces, quotas, or pod diagnostics. A
container that cannot see a GPU suggests the runtime idx_4c6b31b3 boundary and GPU-access
configuration. A model portability requirement suggests ONNX, while a GPU inference
optimization requirement suggests TensorRT.
Multi-tenant isolation can point to different answers depending on the boundary. MIG creates
hardware-isolated GPU instances on supported GPUs. vGPU presents virtual GPU resources to
virtual machines through a hypervisor. BlueField and DOCA can enforce network, storage, and
security controls around tenants. The stem must indicate which layer requires isolation.
Monitoring language also requires precision. NVIDIA-SMI provides a quick local snapshot.
DCGM provides fleet health, telemetry, policy, and diagnostics. Prometheus stores and queries
time-series metrics, while Grafana presents dashboards. Nsight Systems exposes the CPU-GPU
timeline, and Nsight Compute provides kernel-level analysis.
Once the layer is identified, compare the answer choices according to the problem they solve
rather than according to how familiar they look.

Dealing with false positives in content filters
A false positive happens idx_b70fb86b when a guardrail blocks or flags a response that was actually safe and
appropriate. In low-volume systems, this is an inconvenience. In enterprise systems,
processing thousands of interactions daily, a miscalibrated filter can quietly degrade usability
to the point where users stop trusting the system — or start working around it.
Consider a concrete example: a legal services firm deploys an internal assistant to help
paralegals research case precedents. The content safety filter is configured at maximum
severity for violence-related content — a reasonable default for most applications. Within the
first week, the team notices the assistant is refusing to summarize court cases involving
assault, manslaughter, or wrongful death — all entirely legitimate queries for the use case. The
filter cannot distinguish between a user asking how to commit violence and a paralegal asking
for a case summary that involves violence. Both trigger the same category at the same severity
level.
This is a domain mismatch, not a model failure. The filter was calibrated for a general
consumer context and applied without adjustment to a specialized professional context. The
result: legitimate users hit walls on routine work, and the system's perceived reliability drops.
Here is how to address false positives systematically rather than reactively:
Audit guardrail activation logs weekly during the first month post-launch. Categorize
activations as true positives (correctly blocked harmful content) versus false positives
(blocked legitimate content). If your false positive rate exceeds 5% of total activations,
the filter needs recalibration for your domain.
Adjust severity thresholds by category, not globally. In Microsoft Foundry, guardrail
severity is configurable per risk category. For the legal services example: violence
severity can be lowered from maximum to medium for this specific deployment, while
hate and self-harm categories remain at maximum. This surgical adjustment reduces
false positives without opening the system to genuinely harmful content.
Use blocklists to add precision where broad filters are too blunt. If the filter is blocking
specific terms that are legitimate in your domain, a blocklist configured in allowlist
mode can explicitly permit those terms. This is more maintainable than loosening
broad severity thresholds.
Document every threshold adjustment with a rationale. Guardrail tuning decisions are
compliance-relevant. If an auditor asks why violence detection is set to medium
severity, the answer should be in a versioned configuration document, not someone's
memory.

We need to begin by idx_e3c3eb89idx_654dc7d5 discussing Docker Production Hardening.
Three hardening requirements apply to every inference container idx_803f8e1aidx_94ae9019 in production. First, use a
named persistent volume for model weight caches (e.g., --mount type=volume,src=model-
cache,dst=/models) so that pod restarts do not re-download multi-gigabyte weights from the
registry. Second, set explicit CPU and memory resource limits in addition to GPU limits: a
container without CPU limits can starve other workloads on the node during batch-processing
spikes. Third, run the inference server as a non-root user: add RUN useradd -m inference &&
USER inference to the Dockerfile and verify with docker run --rm your-image id that UID is not
0. These three requirements are enforced by the admission webhook in the reference Helm
chart in the companion repository.
The most expensive failure mode in a production inference deployment is a pod that starts,
passes all health probes, joins the load balancer, and then crashes on the first real request
because the GPU driver version does not match, the model file is corrupted, or the available
VRAM is 2 GB short of what the model requires. A startup check script catches all of these
before the pod becomes ready.

KEDA Autoscaling on Inference-Specific Metrics
The built-in Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales on CPU idx_d3b89b0aidx_4fc4ebdc and memory. For inference

while the GPU is fully saturated and requests are queuing. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven

To query relational idx_48769643 databases, you use a special language called a structured query language,
or SQL for short. SQL is used to interact with databases, enabling you to idx_5b540c18 create tables and
relationships, insert, update, and delete data in tables, and run queries across multiple tables.
Typical databases that utilize the SQL language include MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and
Oracle.
Relational databases are also idx_1b702a49 referred to as Online Transaction Processing (OLTP) databases.
This type of database is designed for transactional workloads, which involve frequently
adding, updating, and deleting small amounts of data. A common term idx_6cc88dda used in this context is
CRUD, which stands for Create, Read, Update, and Delete.
Relational idx_0dc197be databases, or Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS), perform
these CRUD operations in response to requests from your applications. Examples of
transactional applications include an e-commerce website that processes customer orders or
an employee database used by an HR application.
In the next section, you idx_ef349b0a will learn more about Relational Databases on AWS.
Working with relational databases on AWS
Relational idx_7374818a databases, such as MySQL or Microsoft SQL idx_0265d443 Server, must run on a compute resource,
such as an Amazon EC2 instance. You need to install the database engine, after which you can
interact with it idx_8a50768e using idx_893737e9 either a command-line interface (CLI) or a graphical user interface
(GUI).
It's important to understand that a relational database requires core infrastructure
components—compute, storage, and network connectivity—to be accessible and usable by
your applications.
While installing and configuring a database engine like MySQL or Oracle on an EC2 instance is
a valid approach, AWS offers a fully managed solution called Amazon Relational Database
Service (Amazon RDS). Amazon idx_086dd37d RDS is an OLTP database designed for transaction-based
workloads, such as student enrolment applications for universities or databases used in e-
commerce applications. As another example related to the client requirements of Belly Brew
Co. Limited, Amazon RDS can be used to host stock inventory data for its gut-friendly
beverages, which will be updated regularly as orders are fulfilled and stock is replenished.

Common Pitfalls in Production AI Deployment
The following are common pitfalls idx_d118779eidx_33c44cd6 one encounters in production AI deployment:
Baking Model Weights into the Docker Image
Problem: A team packages a 15 GB model file inside the Docker image. The registry push
takes 45 minutes. A rollback requires another 45-minute pull. The CI pipeline times
out.
Fix: Mount model weights from a PersistentVolumeClaim or object storage bucket at
runtime. Keep container images under 3 GB. Separate the model artifact lifecycle from
the code lifecycle—they change at different rates and need independent versioning.
Scaling on CPU Utilisation for GPU Workloads
Problem: The HPA is configured with a CPU target of 70%. GPU inference pods run at
6% CPU while the GPU is fully saturated and requests are queuing for 30 seconds. The
autoscaler never fires.
Fix: Use KEDA with Prometheus triggers on infer_queue_depth and p95 latency.
Remove the CPU-based HPA for any pod that does its real work on a GPU. CPU is a valid
autoscaling signal only for CPU-bound inference workloads.
Deploying a Quantized Model Without Quality Evaluation
Problem: A team switches from FP16 to Q4_K_M to save VRAM costs. The model now
produces incorrect commands in 20% of Linux administration prompts because Q4
loses precision in technical vocabulary. Engineers report that the assistant 'got
dumber'.
Fix: Run quantize_and_evaluate.py before every format change. The keyword_hit_rate
gate (≥ 90% for PRODUCTION_READY) exists precisely to catch this. Never ship a
quantized model based on latency and cost metrics alone.
Ignoring VRAM Headroom and Triggering OOM Kills
Problem: A team sets gpu_memory_fraction=0.95 to maximise utilisation. When a
long-context request arrives, the model exceeds the allocation, the CUDA runtime
raises an OOM error, and the pod crashes. Kubernetes restarts it, clearing all warm
VRAM state and causing a 60-second service gap.
Fix: Set gpu_memory_fraction to 0.85 or lower. The 15% headroom absorbs context
length variation and prevents OOM crashes. Monitor infer_gpu_memory_used_bytes
and alert at 90%: not 100%. The startup_check.py from Section 9.1 warns if headroom
is under 1 GB at launch.

However, backups are typically performed at regular intervals, such as every four hours or
daily. Determining how often you should back up your data requires an understanding of your
Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO).
These two parameters will help you design a recovery strategy that meets your business
requirements:
RTO: This represents idx_0c5c0b52 the amount of time (in hours) it takes to recover from a disaster
and return to a working state. The recovery time includes provisioning a new database
instance and performing a restore operation, which depends on the volume of data
being restored.
RPO: This defines the idx_0eb7f687 amount of data (measured as a factor of time) you are willing to
lose in the event of a disaster. For example, if you cannot afford to lose more than four
hours of data, then you must back up your data at least every four hours. The shorter
the RPO, the less data is at risk of being lost during a failure.
Based on your RTO and RPO requirements, you can define your backup strategy. Amazon RDS
offers two types of backup options: automatic backups and manual snapshots.
Automatic backups are generated idx_427a1fdd and managed by AWS. When enabled, these
backups occur daily, and AWS provides a maximum retention period of 35 days. You
can configure the retention period between 1 and 35 days. Older backups are
automatically deleted after the set retention period. You can restore your database from
these automatic backups at any time within the retention window. When you delete
your database, AWS automatically deletes the associated automatic backups.
Manual snapshots require you to initiate the backup manually. You should do this
before making a significant change to your application or database, so you have a
recent backup to revert to in case of failure. Unlike automatic backups, manual
snapshots are not automatically deleted — you must manually delete them when they
are no longer needed. Additionally, backups can be copied across AWS regions,
allowing you to restore a copy of your database in another region if necessary.
AWS stores backups of your database in Amazon S3. You do not have direct access to these
buckets. Instead, you must perform a restore operation from Amazon RDS to restore from
backups.
While backups and restores enable you to recover from disasters such as a database instance
failure, they do not provide high availability. Restoring a backup can take time, depending on
the size of the database, which may result in your customers being unable to access the
application until the restore process is fully complete. To address this limitation, AWS offers a
feature known as multi-AZ deployments, which is idx_dabf5c1e discussed in the next section.

Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment
Amazon RDS also idx_d30b3afe offers the Multi-AZ DB Cluster deployment feature, which provides
additional capabilities compared to the Multi-AZ instance deployment option. In this
configuration, replication is semi-synchronous —meaning the primary DB instance waits for
at least one replica (not necessarily all) to acknowledge receipt of the data, though not
necessarily confirmation of durability (i.e., writing the data to disk). This approach improves idx_725a23f5
durability over asynchronous replication while reducing the performance impact typically
associated with fully synchronous replication.
According to the diagram in Figure 9.8, the Multi-AZ DB Cluster deployment consists of two
read-replica DB instances, in addition to the primary writeable DB instance.
Figure 9.8: Amazon RDS multi-AZ DB cluster
255 Databases on AWS
These three instances are distributed across three separate Availability Zones, providing high
availability, increased read capacity, and lower write latency compared to the multi-AZ DB
instance deployment.
Amazon RDS offers a single writable instance of your database by default. This means that the
primary master copy of the database must be online and accessible to commit any write
operations. As a Cloud Practitioner, you must consider how well your database can scale to
handle increasing idx_945ae457 load. For relational databases, such as Amazon RDS, running idx_1d5627ff engines like
MySQL or PostgreSQL, you can only scale out your read requests using a feature known as read
replicas. This is discussed in the next section.
Amazon RDS read replicas
An Amazon RDS Read Replica is idx_25ac5128 a read-only copy of a database that applications can use to
perform read queries. The replica is created by taking a snapshot of the primary instance and
launching a new read-only instance from that snapshot. Asynchronous replication from the
primary database to the read replica ensures that data changes committed to the primary
instance are eventually reflected on the replica.
This setup reduces the load on the primary database by offloading read traffic to the replicas. It
also enables continued support for read queries during planned maintenance on the primary
instance.
As shown in Figure 9.9, you can create multiple read replicas from a single primary DB instance,
allowing you to scale out your read workloads to meet increasing demand.

Amazon Aurora is AWS's proprietary MySQL-compatible and PostgreSQL-compatible

The DB cluster is composed of two types of DB instances:
Primary DB instance: Supports both read and write operations and performs all data
modifications to the cluster volume. The primary instance is accessible via the cluster
endpoint.
Aurora Replicas: You can create up to 15 Aurora Replicas in addition to the primary
instance. Although these replicas connect to the same cluster volume, they are used
only for read operations. Applications can connect to them via the reader endpoint.
Aurora Replicas are designed to handle read queries and can also be used for failover if the
primary instance fails.
When provisioning Amazon Aurora, you must select a DB instance class, which can be either
burstable or memory-optimized, with various instance types offering different levels of CPU,
memory, and idx_d56ee303 network idx_47ba74db capacity. Additionally, Amazon Aurora is also available as a serverless
option, which is discussed in the next section.
Amazon Aurora Serverless
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 is a fully managed service that includes built-in autoscaling
capabilities, allowing it to idx_6a95d542 automatically adjust database capacity based on workload patterns
and application demand. You are charged only for the resources consumed by your DB cluster,
helping you avoid overprovisioning unless explicitly required by your application.
You do not need to specify the instance class, type, or size for your Aurora Serverless database.
Instead, you define Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs), which Amazon Aurora uses to provision the
required capacity. Each ACU provides approximately 2 GiB of memory along with a
corresponding amount of CPU and network bandwidth. You specify a minimum and maximum
number of ACUs for your cluster, and Amazon Aurora will scale within this range—adding or
removing capacity based on application load.
Interestingly, the ACU count can scale down to zero, allowing the cluster to pause after a
period of inactivity. This can be highly cost-efficient, as when your cluster is paused, you are
only charged for the storage consumed.
Aurora Serverless is ideal for development and testing environments, as well as production
workloads with unpredictable usage patterns. For example, an e-commerce website might
experience increased traffic during the winter or rainy seasons. Another use case is deploying a
new web application when its popularity is still uncertain. Once usage trends are clearer, you
can decide whether to transition to a standard Aurora deployment or continue using the
serverless architecture.

Migrating databases with AWS Database Migration

Amazon offers the Database Migration Service (DMS), which is commonly used to help
businesses idx_026cd73f migrate their idx_0e250933 on-premises databases to the AWS Cloud. You can migrate existing

AWS DMS, AWS helps you to configure a source endpoint for the source database and a target
endpoint for your target database. Using replication, the data and any changes are migrated
across to the target database. When you are ready to switch over, you simply point your
application to the new target database endpoint.
You can perform a one-time migration or even configure continuous replication to migrate
ongoing changes from your on-premises database over a defined period.

Homogeneous migrations, such as MySQL to MySQL or Oracle to Oracle

migration.
AWS DMS simplifies database migrations by reducing the complexity, risk, and downtime
traditionally associated with moving databases to the cloud. Whether you are migrating
between similar database engines or converting to a different database platform, AWS DMS
provides a managed solution that helps you transfer data securely and efficiently. By
combining AWS DMS with the AWS Schema Conversion Tool for heterogeneous migrations,

Pushing container images
The act of pushing container images to a container registry is handled by the container tool
that we are using, which respects the OCI Distribution Specification.
In this idx_0a58d0ea process, the blobs, which are the binary form of the content, are uploaded first, and,
usually at the end, the manifest is then uploaded. This order idx_d6bcf23f is not strict and mandatory by the
specification, but a registry may refuse a manifest that references blobs that it does not know.
Using a container management tool to push a container image to a registry, we must again
specify the name of the repository in the form shown before and the container image's tag we
want to upload.
Tag management
As introduced in Chapter 4, Managing Running Containers, container images are identified by a
name idx_016c66c6 and a tag. Thanks to the tag mechanism, we can store several different versions of the
container images on a system's local cache or on a container registry.
The container idx_b5c89187 registry should be able to expose the feature of content discovery, providing the
list of the container images' tags to the client requesting it. This feature can give the
opportunity to the container registry's users to choose the right container image to pull and
run on the target systems.
Pulling container images
In the process of pulling container images, the client first requests the manifest to identify the
blobs, which are idx_393de1ac the binary form of the content, to pull to get the final idx_a0268181 container image. The
order is strict because, without pulling and parsing the manifest file of the container image, the
client would not be able to know which binary data it has to request from the registry.
Using a container management tool to pull a container image from a registry, we have to use
the fully-qualified name of the image, which includes both tag and repository.
Authentication management
All the previous idx_d3402df3 operations may require authentication. In many idx_36e25df9 cases, public container
registries may allow anonymous pulling and content discovery, but for pushing container
images, they require a valid authentication.
Depending on the container registry chosen, we might find basic or advanced features to
authenticate to a container registry. This lets our client store a token and then use it for every
operation that could require it.

features to meet modern application requirements. Amazon Aurora provides six copies of the
database using a clustered storage solution spread across three Availability Zones and includes
advanced features such as self-healing capabilities.
You learned about the importance of designing your database solution for high availability
using multi-AZ deployments and for scaling read operations using read replicas. You also

applications, where applications require single-digit millisecond latency and data structures
need to be flexible without a strict schema. This NoSQL offering from AWS also includes
advanced features such as a built-in in-memory caching service called DynamoDB
Accelerator (DAX) and the ability to deploy a multi-master (multi-active) database solution
across multiple regions.
In addition, you learned about Amazon ElastiCache, which provides in-memory caching
engines such as Redis and Memcached. For data warehousing solutions, AWS offers the
Amazon Redshift service, available both as a provisioned cluster and as a serverless solution.
Amazon Redshift Spectrum also allows you to query data stored in Amazon S3 directly, without
having to import it into a Redshift cluster.
Finally, you learned about the AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), which enables
migration of on-premises databases using both homogeneous and heterogeneous migration
options. The latter requires the use of the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT). DMS supports
both one-time migrations and ongoing replication from a source database to a destination
database.

High Availability, Fault Tolerance,
and Elasticity on AWS
Businesses strive to ensure that their software applications are always available and experience
minimal downtime. This is particularly critical when end customers need access to those
applications, such as customers of an e-commerce business. Any downtime can impact not
only sales but also the company's reputation. Therefore, designing solutions that are highly
available or even fault-tolerant is essential for most businesses.
If you deploy your application on a single EC2 instance supported by a single database
instance, you create a single point of failure. If there are idx_76295bc9 any hardware or software issues with
the EC2 instance, or if the Availability Zone in which it is deployed goes offline, your customers
will be unable to access the application. Modern architectural patterns, therefore, incorporate
high availability into their idx_1ee3d5fa design. This often involves having multiple EC2 instances serving
the same application, ideally deployed across multiple Availability Zones (AZs) within a
region.
Using the multi-AZ option for your Amazon RDS database is another example of avoiding
single points of failure. If your primary instance fails, AWS performs a failover to the standby
instance, which maintains an up-to-date copy of your data. Your RDS database remains highly
available, although there may be a few seconds of downtime during the failover process.
Fault tolerance takes this concept one idx_0520dfe0 step further, ensuring that your application continues
to operate even if a component fails. In this case, Amazon RDS Multi-AZ alone is insufficient, as
the failover process still introduces a brief period of downtime. Instead, you might re-architect
your solution to use DynamoDB Global Tables, which offer the level of fault tolerance required.
If a region goes offline, traffic can be redirected to another region with a copy of the DynamoDB
table, maintaining seamless access.
You also want your application to be scalable, ensuring you have sufficient resources to handle
changes in demand. You must be able to scale out as demand increases and scale in as it
decreases. Scaling out may involve adding more EC2 instances to your fleet and distributing
the load across the increased compute capacity. Conversely, when demand drops, you want to
scale back and terminate unused EC2 instances to reduce costs and avoid waste. This ability to
dynamically adjust resources in response to idx_e94b0be1 fluctuating demand is known as elasticity.

One of the areas where AI-assisted tasks shine the most is writing code. Compared to human
languages, computer languages are much easier for computers to master. Computer program-
ming languages, such as Python, are designed to be unambiguous and highly structured. Each
statement, parameter, or keyword follows a clearly defined grammar and syntax rules. If we miss a
closing bracket or a comma, the program will simply fail to run until we correct the syntax mistake.
On the other hand, human languages are ambiguous and rely heavily on cultural and contextual
references. Take the following sentence as an example: “Eric writes code in Python; it is his fa-
vorite coding language.” To English speakers, the “it” in the second part of the sentence naturally
refers to the language ‘Python,’ but it is a (surprisingly) difficult task for computers to know that
contextual reference with accuracy.
This is why coding assistance was one of the first areas where AI LLMs really shone. Often re -
ferred to as vibe coding in the community, it generally refers to the translation layer of converting
humans’ ambiguous and unstructured natural language tasks into computer code. When we
are brainstorming or prototyping, we can describe our thoughts to this vibe code tool, and it will

racter can have two different meanings, depending on its placement in the regular expression. See

In this command, the '^[^a-zA-Z]' regular expression means to look for all lines that do not begin

Loosely coupled components
The best i d x _ 7 9 c 1 3 f b a way to address a complex subject has always been to divide it into smaller subproblems that are more
manageable. As an example, it would be insanely complex to build a house in a single step. It is much easier to
build a house from simple parts that are then combined into the final result.
The same also applies i d x _ d 5 1 b 3 2 c 6 to software development. It is much easier to develop a very complex application if we divide
this application into smaller components that interoperate and make up the overall application. Now, it is much
easier to develop these components individually if they are loosely coupled with each other. What this means is
that component A makes no assumptions about the inner workings of, say, components B and C, and is only
interested in how it can communicate with those two components across well-defined interfaces.
If each component has a well-defined and simple public interface through which communication with the other
components in the system and the outside world happens, then this enables us to develop each component
individually, without implicit dependencies on other components. During the development process, other
components in the system can easily be replaced by stubs or mocks to allow us to test our components.
Stateful versus stateless
Every meaningful i d x _ 8 a 5 6 6 f f 7 business application creates, modifies, or uses data. In IT, a synonym for data is state. An
application service that creates or modifies persistent data is i d x _ 4 2 0 e 7 3 1 e called a stateful component. Typical stateful
components are database services or services that create files. On the other hand, application components i d x _ 9 b 4 d c 9 2 1 that do
not create or modify persistent data are called stateless components.
In a distributed application i d x _ 9 1 b e d f 0 0 architecture, stateless components are much simpler to handle than stateful
components. Stateless components can easily be scaled up and down. Furthermore, they can be quickly and
painlessly torn down and restarted on a completely different node of the cluster—all because they have no
persistent data associated with them.
Given this, it is helpful to design a system in a way that most of the application services are stateless. It is best to
push all the stateful components to the boundaries of the application and limit how many are used. Managing
stateful components is hard.

Routing
Routing i d x _ 3 b 9 5 e 2 b 1 is the mechanism of sending packets of data from a source component to a target component. Routing is
categorized into different types. The so-called OSI model (see the reference to this in the Further reading section at
the end of this chapter for more information) is used to distinguish between different types of routing. In the
context of containers and container orchestration, routing at layers 2, 3, 4, and 7 is relevant. We will look at routing
in more detail in subsequent chapters. For now, let's just say that layer 2 routing is the most low-level type of
routing, which connects a MAC address to another MAC address, while layer 7 routing, which is also called
application-level routing, is the most high-level one. The latter is, for example, used to route requests that have a
target identifier—that is, a URL such as https://acme.com/pets —to the appropriate target component in our
system.
Load balancing
Load balancing i d x _ b c 7 6 8 0 f 9 is used whenever Service A needs to communicate with Service B, such as in a request-response
pattern, but the latter is running in more than one instance, as shown in the following diagram:
Figure 9.5 – The request of Service A is being load-balanced to Service B
If we have i d x _ 7 0 d 8 0 9 6 f multiple instances of a service, such as Service B, running in our system, we want to make sure that
every one of those instances gets an equal amount of workload assigned to it. This task is a generic one, which
means that we don't want the caller to have to do the load balancing but, rather, an external service that intercepts
the call and takes over the role of deciding i d x _ 6 f b 0 5 d 9 6 which of the target service instances to forward the call to. This external
service is called a load balancer. Load balancers can use different algorithms to decide how to distribute incoming
calls to target service instances. The most common algorithm that's used is called round-robin. This algorithm
assigns requests repetitively, starting with instance 1, then 2, until instance n. After the last instance has been
served, the load balancer starts over with instance number 1.
In the preceding example, a load balancer also facilitates high availability since a request from Service A will be
forwarded to a healthy instance of Service B. The load balancer also takes the role of periodically checking the
health of each instance of Service B.

To avoid i d x _ 0 2 0 e e 6 c 8 downtime when one of the many components in the system fails, each part of the system needs to be
redundant. This includes the application components, as well as all infrastructure parts. What that means is that if
we have a payment service as part of our application, then we need to run this service redundantly. The easiest way
to do that is to run multiple instances of this very service on different nodes of our cluster. The same applies, say, to
an edge router or a load balancer. We cannot afford for this to ever go down. Thus, the router or load balancer must
be redundant.
Health checks
We i d x _ 1 1 5 d 5 6 7 2 have mentioned various times that in a i d x _ a 8 b 1 0 b c 9 distributed application architecture, with its many parts, the failure of
an individual component is highly likely and it is only a matter of time until it happens. For that reason, we must
run every single component of the system redundantly. Load balancers then distribute the traffic across the
individual instances of a service.
But now, there is another problem. How does the load balancer or router know whether a certain service instance is
available? It could have crashed, or it could be unresponsive. To solve this problem, we can use i d x _ 1 8 3 9 b a 4 f so-called health
checks. The load balancer, or some other system service on its behalf, periodically polls all the service instances
and checks their health. The questions are basically, Are you still there? Are you healthy? The answer to each service
is either Yes or No, or the health check times out if the instance is not responsive anymore.
If the component answers with No or a timeout occurs, then the system kills the corresponding instance and spins
up a new instance in its place. If all this happens in a fully automated way, then we say that we have an auto-
healing system in place. Instead of the load balancer periodically polling the status of the components,
responsibility can also be turned around. The components could be required to periodically send live signals to the
load balancer. If a component fails to send live signals over a predefined, extended period, it is assumed to be
unhealthy or dead.
There are situations where either of the described ways is more appropriate.

Canary releases
Canary releases i d x _ a 2 0 2 2 7 2 f are releases where we have the current version of the application service and the new version
installed on the system in parallel. As such, they resemble blue-green deployments. At first, all traffic is still routed
through the current version. We then configure a router so that it funnels a small percentage, say, 1%, of the overall
traffic to the new version of the application service. Subsequently, the behavior of the new service is monitored
closely to find out whether it works as expected. If all the criteria for success are met, then the router is configured
to funnel more traffic, say, 5% this time, through the new service. Again, the behavior of the new service is closely
monitored and, if it is successful, more and more traffic is routed to it until we reach 100%. Once all the traffic has
been routed to the new service and it has been stable for some time, the old version of the service can be
decommissioned.
Why do we call this a canary release? It is named after the system where coal miners would use canary birds as an
early warning in the mines. Canary birds are particularly sensitive to toxic gas, and if a canary bird died, the miners
knew they had to abandon the mine immediately.
Irreversible data changes
If part of our i d x _ 6 2 6 8 a d 3 1 update process is to execute an irreversible change in our state, such as an irreversible schema change
in a backing relational database, then we need to address this with special care. It is possible to execute such
changes without downtime if we use the right approach. It is important to recognize that, in such a situation, we
cannot deploy the code changes that require the new data structure in the data store at the same time as the
changes to the data. Rather, the whole update has to be separated into three distinct steps. In the first step, we roll
out a backward-compatible schema and data change. If this is successful, then we roll out the new code in the
second step. Again, if that is successful, we clean up the schema in the third step and remove the backward
compatibility:

Modern microservice patterns
Microservices i d x _ e 3 b 3 7 c 6 1 have evolved significantly since their inception, building on the foundational principles of
distributed architectures to address scalability, resilience, and rapid iteration in modern applications. In essence, a
microservice architecture decomposes an application into small, independently deployable services, each focused
on a single business capability. This approach contrasts with monoliths by enabling teams to develop, deploy, and
scale services autonomously, often using Docker containers for encapsulation and portability. However, as systems
grow, specific patterns emerge to handle common challenges such as inter-service communication, data
consistency, and observability.
One key modern pattern is the API gateway, which acts as a single entry point for clients, routing requests to
appropriate microservices while handling concerns such as authentication, rate limiting, and request aggregation.
For example, in a Dockerized setup, an API gateway container can front multiple backend services, reducing client
complexity and enhancing security. Another essential pattern is Saga, used for managing distributed transactions
across services without traditional two-phase commits. In Saga, a sequence of local transactions is coordinated via
events or commands; if one fails, compensating actions roll back prior steps, ensuring eventual consistency in e-
commerce flows such as order processing.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) separates read and write operations into distinct models,
allowing optimized scaling—for instance, read-heavy services can use cached views while writes update the
source of truth. Paired with Event Sourcing, where changes are stored as immutable events rather than direct state
updates, this enables robust auditing and replayability, which is ideal for financial or auditing-intensive apps. The

Answers
Here are the possible answers to this chapter's questions:
In a distributed application architecture, every piece of the software and infrastructure needs to be
redundant in a production environment, where the continuous uptime of the application is mission-
critical. A highly distributed application consists of many parts, and the likelihood of one of the pieces
failing or misbehaving increases with the number of parts. It is guaranteed that, given enough time,
every part will eventually fail. To avoid outages of the application, we need redundancy in every part, be
it a server, a network switch, or a service running on a cluster node in a container.
In highly distributed, scalable, and fault-tolerant systems, individual services of the application can
move around due to scaling needs or due to component failures. Thus, we cannot hardwire different
services with each other. Service A, which needs access to Service B, should not have to know details
about Service B, such as its IP address. It should rely on an external provider for this information. DNS is
such a provider of location information. Service A just tells it that it wants to talk to Service B and the
DNS service will figure out the details.
A circuit breaker is a means to avoid cascading failures if a component in a distributed application is
failing or misbehaving. Similar to a circuit breaker in electric wiring, a software-driven circuit breaker
cuts the communication between a client and a failed service. The circuit breaker will directly report an
error back to the client component if the failed service is called. This allows the system to recover or heal
from failure.
A monolithic application is easier to manage than a multi-service application since it consists of a single
deployment package. On the other hand, a monolith is often harder to scale to account for increased
demand in one particular area of the application. In a distributed application, each service can be scaled
individually, and each service can run on optimized infrastructure, while a monolith needs to run on
infrastructure that is OK for all or most of the features implemented in it. However, over time, this has

Logging is essential in distributed applications for capturing operational details across multiple
components, enabling developers and operators to diagnose issues, track request flows, and analyze
system behavior in complex, dispersed environments where live debugging is impractical. However,
costs must be considered, as verbose logging can consume significant storage and network bandwidth
and incur expenses in cloud solutions, requiring a balance between detail and efficiency. Additionally,
sensitive data such as PII, PHI, and SFI should never be logged to avoid compliance violations and

Ports
The traffic rules take into account the protocol and port that is being filtered, so you can make
more granular rules that specify the traffic in more detail. For instance, you can separate rules
for traffic using Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), User Datagram Protocol (UDP), Stream
Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP), or Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP).
A firewalld port defines a protocol port number (i.e., 80) or a port range (8080-8082) and a
protocol (TCP, UDP, STCP, or DCCP).
Services
A firewalld service is a port or group of ports configured together to allow a system service to
work properly. Many applications require more than one port to be open simultaneously, and
services allow you to manage them together as a single unit.

we need it.

The following idx_34a4ab55 example shows how to create a self-signed certificate with the openssl utility:
$ mkdir certs
$ openssl req -newkey rsa:4096 -x509 -sha256 -nodes \

certificate are written inside the certs directory.

The first category begins with tasks where natural language is used to retrieve, generate, or guide
the creation of code.
Text-to-code tasks
Text-to-code tasks take text as input and output code, typically involving scenarios such as code
retrieval, code generation, and numeric programming:
• Code Retrieval: Aims to search for relevant code based on natural language, or to mine
parallel text-code pairs from unannotated corpora. This task is usually accomplished
by computing the similarity between the query and candidate code embeddings, and
contextual embeddings produced by bidirectional language models (such as BERT) have
been proven to be very useful.
• Code Generation: Aims to generate code based on natural language descriptions, typically
functions or methods. This task can be seen as an upgraded version of code retrieval,
utilizing generative models instead of retrieval models. Statistical Machine Translation
(SMT) and Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have been widely applied to this
task, often with enhanced decoders utilizing the unique syntactic rules of programming
languages. However, pretrained language models based on the Transformer architecture
have changed this landscape, allowing direct source code generation via autoregressive
language modeling even without task-specific fine-tuning.
• Numeric Programming: Numeric programming is also a special case of code generation,
requiring the language model to solve mathematical reasoning problems by generating
code that will be executed by an external interpreter. This task abstracts the reasoning
process from numerical calculation, so this should be given special consideration when
choosing a code LLM or in practice.
After tasks that generate code from text, the next category focuses on transforming, completing,
repairing, or testing existing code.
Text-to-SQL is a special case of code generation, and this approach is sim -
pler. The model generates SQL commands from natural language queries;
compared to general-purpose languages such as Python and C, SQL has
structured characteristics. Therefore, the text-to-SQL approach has been
widely used in data management.

• Assertion Generation: Assertion generation is a task closely related to unit testing. Given a
program and a set of unit tests, the goal of this task is to generate assertions (also known
as oracles in software engineering) so that the program can be evaluated using the unit
tests. This task is not typically the focus of the NLP community, as program generation
tasks for LLM evaluation generally involve independent, competitive approaches, where
simply asserting that the program output matches the expected answer suffices.
• Mutation Generation: The purpose of mutation generation is to produce mutants of
a given program for mutation testing, which is closely related to unit test generation
and assertion generation. Mutants that are not detected by a given set of unit tests and
assertions indicate the need for additional test cases or better assertions. Masking tokens
in the source code and sampling from the output of masked language models has become
a common approach for this task.
• Fuzz Testing: Fuzz testing aims to mutate a given set of unit tests to generate new test cases
and is another task related to software testing. While much of the fuzzing work targets
deep learning libraries, very few have utilized language models to carry out this process.
• Type Prediction: Aims to predict types in dynamic programming languages such as Python
and JavaScript. It has been used as a pre-training objective for code LLMs and is often
simplified to a binary tagging task to predict which tokens in the code are identifiers.
Some downstream tasks move in the opposite direction, using code as the input and producing
natural language descriptions, reviews, or labels.
Code-to-text tasks
Code-to-text tasks take code as input and output text, typically including scenarios such as code
summarization, code review, and identifier prediction.
• Code Summarization: Code summarization, also known as docstring generation, aims
to generate a natural language description for a given piece of code (usually a function
or method). This is the exact opposite of code generation, and SMT/NMT techniques
are also applied here.
• Code Review: Code review aims to automate the process of peer code reviews, and it comes
in various forms. Many early studies formulated it as a binary classification task to accept
or reject modifications upon submission, while other studies used information retrieval
techniques to recommend comments from existing comment repositories. However, as
generative models have become more powerful, researchers have also explored directly
generating review comments as a sequence-to-sequence learning task.

Tracing the evolution of code generation and
completion
Code programming assistance technologies have a history of more than 40 years. Their
development has gone through several stages, from syntax highlighting, integration within
integrated development environments (IDEs), to code analysis and specification checks.
Among these, tools such as IDEs have been iconic over the past 20 years. They significantly
improve development efficiency and quality through features like automatic code completion,
code highlighting, syntax error prompts, and code snippets, while also delivering a superior
programming experience to developers.
LLM technologies have achieved remarkable breakthroughs and success in general industries,
especially excelling in natural language processing tasks. General-purpose LLMs typically possess
some programming capabilities. However, since their training data mainly consists of general
natural language texts—while programming languages are more structured, have explicit
syntax rules, and more direct and precise semantics—their performance in code understanding
and generation, which is a specialized field, may be limited to some extent. This characteristic
distinguishes them from general-purpose large models.
To better meet developers’ needs in code-related tasks, LLMs are trained on large-scale code
repositories, learning code snippets, programming patterns, and coding conventions, thus better
understanding code structure and logic and generating code that adheres to syntax and semantic
requirements.
In practice, how to effectively improve the efficiency and quality of software development has
always been a concern in the field of software engineering. Among various approaches, code
generation, and completion technologies are considered important methods for enhancing
software development automation and ensuring quality, attracting widespread attention from
both academia and industry. Code generation and completion refers to using certain techniques
to automatically generate source code for software, aiming to enable automatic programming
based on user requirements. This greatly reduces developers’ development burden and allows
them to focus more on delivering business value.
In academia, code generation and completion is an important branch of program synthesis,
aiming to assist, or even replace, programmers in writing code. Automatic generation of front-end
code is divided into two approaches: view code and logic code. Common solutions for generating
view code include automatic generation from design drafts, such as imgcook. Common schemes
for generating logic code include visual orchestration-based generation, input-output sample-
based generation, code corpus-based generation, and function description-based generation.

Continuous Access Evaluation
Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) keeps access decisions alive instead of fixed at sign-in.
It lets apps idx_a8f3dce6 check back with Entra ID whenever something meaningful changes like risk,
location, or device posture so sessions stay aligned with real-time conditions. CAE turns
identity from a one-time check into an ongoing, adaptive trust signal. For example, a user signs
in to Outlook from their corporate network. Later, they walk next door and connect their
laptop to the café's public Wi-Fi. Without CAE, their Outlook session would continue because
Conditional Access was only evaluated at sign-in. With CAE, Entra detects the shift to an
untrusted network and signals Outlook to re-check the session immediately. Outlook forces re-
authentication, Conditional Access is re-evaluated, and access is either blocked or MFA-
challenged in near real-time without waiting for token expiry.
For CAE to work the client must be CAE-capable, the workload must support CAE and
Microsoft Entra ID must send real-time signals. SharePoint Online, Exchange Online, Teams,
and Microsoft Graph already support CAE and enforce real-time Conditional Access decisions.
Organizations can enable their applications for CAE by using CAE-aware authentication
libraries (like MSAL) and implement logic to handle CAE-specific error responses from the
resource API, prompting the app to re-authenticate when Entra ID signals that conditions have
changed.
CAE is auto enabled in all Microsoft Entra tenants. Organizations wishing to disable it can do
so using the session control in Conditional Access policies. Disabling CAE only works when
applied to all applications. It can, however, be applied to all users or selected users and groups.

Understanding encryption mechanisms and capabilities
Before diving into the specific details, let’s first review the different encryption types and Azure-re -
lated capabilities:
• Encryption at rest: This type of encryption safeguards data at rest (stored) by ensuring it
remains unreadable if the storage device is stolen or accessed with malicious intent. Most
Azure services let you Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) or, by default, use Microsoft-managed
keys to ensure data at rest is always encrypted. An additional possibility is Host Your
Own Key (HYOK), which means that you generate the keys and store them in hardware
that you control. Be aware that this option is mostly compatible with Infrastructure as a Service.
• Encryption in transit: This type of encryption protects data in motion. For example, when
accessing https://portal.azure.com using a web browser, the client initiates a TLS
connection with the Azure server. During this process, the client verifies the legitimacy
of the server by validating its certificate, and both sides perform a key exchange to derive
a shared symmetric encryption key. This key is then used to encrypt all subsequent data
transmitted between the client and server.
Security Architecture 330
Asymmetric cryptography is used during the handshake to authenticate the server and
secure the key exchange process. Simply put, this type of encryption ensures that someone
sniffing the network would only see encrypted data and not clear text. As for encryption
at rest, Azure services default to Microsoft-managed certificates, but most services let
you Bring Your Own Certificate (BYOC). When using BYOC, you typically store them in
Azure Key Vault and integrate Azure services with Key Vault to let them pull the certificate.
You may Host Your Own Certificate (HYOC) by storing private keys in hardware that you
control. Be aware that this is absolutely not compatible with Azure PaaS services.
• Encryption in use: This type of encryption protects in-memory data. As with the previous
example, without encryption in use, any administrator or system process of a machine
might perform memory inspection and see data in clear text. In Azure, encryption in use
is offered through the broader confidential computing concept.
Encryption at rest and in transit in Azure rely by default on Microsoft-managed keys. This is by far
the easiest way to leverage Azure services. Many companies rely on these defaults and only bring
their own certificates for internet-facing web apps and APIs. From that perspective, it’s worth
noting that Azure Key Vault has built-in integration mechanisms with well-known Certificate
Authorities (CAs), such as GlobalSign and DigiCert, including automatic certificate renewal.

Figure 9.12: Modeling process of RNN model
The paper DeepAM-Migrate APIs with Multi-Modal Sequence to Sequence Learning focuses on using
RNN to learn vector representations that differentiate Java and C# API, and applies these learned
vectors to the API migration task between these two languages to generate code at the API level.
Many researchers have used RNN models for code token prediction and completion, achieving
remarkable results. Most research models code at the word level using RNNs, but due to the large
number of variables in code, learning becomes very challenging; therefore, some work has started
to model code at the character level.
Programming languages exhibit certain local repetitiveness. For example, a defined variable is
often reused later in the code. However, these variables are largely treated as out-of-vocabulary
(OoV) words, usually represented as UNK. Predicting a UNK is of no help to programmers in their
coding, so researchers have considered incorporating pointer network mechanisms into language
models to accurately predict locally repeated words. The pointer network can effectively copy
words that need to be reused from the input code snippet. Pointer networks were first proposed at
the 2015 IEEE conference, originally used to solve combinatorial optimization problems, and are
a variant of neural machine translation models (i.e., sequence-to-sequence models, Seq2Seq
models). In pointer networks, the attention mechanism is simpler, as it does not consider the
input elements, but instead points to them probabilistically.
In 2016, Bhoopchand et al. proposed a Sparse Pointer Network in the paper Learning Python Code
Suggestion with a Sparse Pointer Network, mainly addressing the issue of predicting custom identifiers
(such as class names, method names, variable names, etc.). The paper defines the concept of
“memory” to store the previous K identifiers. The method maintains a vector m=[id1,...,id*K*],
used to record the positions of identifiers in the global vocabulary, i.e., pointers to the global
vocabulary.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 332
At each prediction step, the network combines the global language model distribution, the pointer
probability distribution over custom identifiers, and the current code input to determine the output
word. Compared to traditional recurrent neural networks (without the attention mechanism),
this method increases the accuracy for predicting custom Python identifiers by about 25%.
In their 2018 paper Code Completion with Neural Attention and Pointer Networks, Li et al. proposed
a method for code completion by combining a language model with an attention mechanism
and pointer networks, modeling sequences of abstract syntax trees (ASTs). This model can not
only predict the type of AST nodes but also predict their values, that is, the code to be completed.

Introducing authentication, authorization, and Conditional
Access policies
The terms authentication and authorization are often confused—partly because certain features
straddle both domains.
Authentication is the process whereby a user submits credentials to an identity provider, which
then verifies them. Once successfully validated, the user is signed in.
Authorization determines whether a user or application has permission to access a particular
resource. It’s the responsibility of the resource server to allow or deny access.
This distinction can become blurred with features such as Conditional Access, which intersects
both processes.
For instance, during user sign-in, Conditional Access might prompt for Multi-Factor Authen -
tication (MFA) based on specific conditions (such as login attempts from unfamiliar locations),
but it can also serve as an access gatekeeper—deciding, for example, whether a user can enter
the Azure portal depending on preconfigured rules. Blocking access is more part of the authori -
zation realm than the authentication one. Conditional Access can be seen as the policy engine of
a zero-trust security model that makes decisions based on signals received from devices, users,
networks, and locations.
All of this can contribute to confusion between authentication and authorization.
